ExoNexus | Exploring Beyond Earth 🚀

We are ExoNexus, an interdisciplinary team bringing together Astrobiology and Computer Engineering to solve challenges beyond Earth. We are passionate about space exploration, planetary science, extraterrestrial life, and innovative technology. Our goal is to combine scientific research, computational thinking, and creativity to develop meaningful solutions for space exploration.
summary:
TerraX is an AI-assisted geospatial platform designed to transform Earth into a searchable scientific laboratory for Moon and Mars exploration. It addresses the challenge of discovering terrestrial environments that can serve as analogues for extraterrestrial landscapes by bringing together Earth-observation data and planetary datasets.

The platform enables users to discover potential analogue locations, explore their geological and environmental characteristics, and compare them with selected regions of the Moon and Mars. Its scientific assessment framework considers mineralogy, terrain, temperature, water and ice indicators, dust dynamics, subsurface characteristics and exploration accessibility. A key feature is its Earth–Moon–Mars comparison workflow, demonstrated through a case study connecting India's Rann of Kutch with Mars' Jezero Crater.

By integrating geospatial analysis, AI-assisted similarity assessment and interactive visualisation, TerraX aims to make planetary analogue research more accessible, systematic and data-driven. It can support astrobiological investigations, rover testing, geological research and future mission planning while highlighting the limitations of Earth-based analogues.
details:
TerraX: Earth to Extraterrestrial Analogue Explorer

TerraX is a project developed by Team ExoNexus to explore how different environments on Earth can help us understand the Moon and Mars. The basic idea behind our project is that before exploring other planets, we can learn a lot by studying similar geological environments on our own planet.

TerraX provides a platform to discover and compare potential analogue locations around the world. It focuses on different geological and environmental features, such as rock composition, minerals, terrain, temperature, water and ice indicators, dust activity and surface conditions. These characteristics help us understand how certain places on Earth may be useful for studying extraterrestrial environments.

One of the main examples included in our project is the comparison between the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, India, and Jezero Crater on Mars. The Rann of Kutch has salt-rich surfaces, evaporite deposits and seasonal environmental changes. Studying these features can provide useful insights into geological processes that are also relevant to Martian research.

An important feature of TerraX is its similarity assessment approach. Instead of comparing locations only on the basis of how they look, the project considers seven scientific parameters: geology and mineralogy, terrain and elevation, temperature, water and ice, dust and surface processes, subsurface characteristics and exploration accessibility. These parameters are assigned different weights to create an indicative comparison score.

We also considered the limitations of using Earth as a planetary analogue. Conditions such as gravity, atmospheric pressure, radiation and temperature are very different on other planetary bodies. Therefore, an Earth location cannot be considered an exact replica of Mars or the Moon.

For the technical development, our proposed architecture uses Java for application development and Python for scientific calculations, geospatial analysis and AI-assisted processing. Other planned tools include Spring Boot, FastAPI, NumPy, Pandas, GeoPandas, Rasterio, Scikit-learn, PostgreSQL, PostGIS and Leaflet. The scientific data sources considered include NASA Earthdata, NASA's Planetary Data System and lunar and Martian observation datasets.

What makes TerraX different is its focus on connecting geographical exploration with planetary science. We wanted to create something that goes beyond simply showing locations on a map. Our aim was to make it easier to explore why a particular environment is scientifically relevant, which characteristics make it useful and where its limitations lie.

Through this project, we hope to support future research in astrobiology, planetary geology, rover exploration, surface sampling and the study of environments that may preserve biosignatures.

As Team ExoNexus, our vision is to make Earth a natural laboratory for understanding other worlds and contributing to the future of planetary exploration.
